author: claude
title: Yamanashi's Volcanic Soil and Koshu Skin Contact

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Koshu is often called Japan's own grape. What makes it special?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: It has a long history in Yamanashi, perhaps over a thousand years. The skin has a light pinkish purple color, but traditionally it's made into a pale, delicate white wine.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: I've heard some producers are making Koshu in a different way now.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Yes. Some winemakers use skin contact. Instead of removing the skins right away, they leave the juice with the skins for days or even weeks, like with red wine.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: First, the color. The wine becomes golden or amber. People sometimes call it orange wine. Second, the texture. The skins release phenolic compounds, including tannins, so the wine has more grip in the mouth.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Phenolic grip. So it feels a little like tea?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Exactly, a gentle dryness. It also brings flavors like dried orange peel, ginger and tea leaves.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Does the vineyard matter as well?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Of course. In Yamanashi, many vineyards sit on sloping land around the Kofu Basin, and some areas have volcanic ash soil from nearby mountains. These well-drained soils help in a rainy climate.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So it's a mix of tradition and new ideas.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: That's what I love about it. The same old grape is telling new stories.
